_meta.how_to_regression_diff: Re-run (npm run check:golden scam-radar) — TEST IN A NON-ENGLISH LANGUAGE. v2.1 (2026-09-09) added 8 refinements on top of the v2 rewrite, driven by a live-caught bug: the tool trusted the 'already done?' radio button over contradicting evidence in the visitor's own pasted transcript (case 'en-romance-investment-scam-no-explicit-ask-yet' below is the exact repro — transcript contains '[after reply]' and '[three days of friendly conversation later]' while interactionStatus is 'none'). DO NOT reverse, in addition to every v2 guard already listed in git history for this file: (1) the new top-level 'input_conflict' field ({detected, note}) and the RECONCILE CONFLICTING INPUTS prompt section that populates it — every case below carries this key now, including the two with detected:false; a golden diff tool that requires exact key-set parity will need this key present in ALL cases, not just the conflict one. (2) the code-side stripEmptyItems() backstop (rule 7) — strips blank strings/objects out of every array before the guard or the response ever sees them; do not remove it even though the prompt also forbids empty bullets directly. (3) the observable-wording-vs-sender-intent, no-universal-genuine-sender-behavior, no-certain-next-stage-prediction, offered-platform-is-not-controlled-platform, and pattern-labeled-as-pattern (not fact) prompt sections — all five are new outputGuard prohibit entries too; removing the prompt section without removing the guard entry just means the guard silently repairs what the prompt should have prevented, which is strictly worse for latency with no behavior difference the visitor would notice, so keep both or neither.

input.messageText:
Subject: URGENT: Your account has been suspended — verify now

Dear Valued Customer,

We have detected unusual activity on your account. Your access has been temporarily suspended for your protection.

To restore full access, you must verify your identity within 24 HOURS or your account will be permanently deleted.

Click here to verify: http://secure-paypa1-verify.com/restore

You will need to provide:
- Full name and date of birth
- Credit card number and CVV
- Social Security Number

PayPal Security Team

output.verdict_explanation: The message combines several strong warning signs: a sender domain that substitutes a digit for a letter to resemble a known brand, a link with the same substitution, a 24-hour deletion threat, and a request for a credit card number, CVV, and Social Security Number through that link. You have also already entered a password or code into a page reached through this message, which makes prompt action on your real account important.

scam_pattern.label: Phishing / Account Impersonation
scam_pattern.explanation: This message fits a common pattern in which a sender impersonates a financial service, creates urgency through a suspension or deletion threat, and directs the recipient to a lookalike site to harvest login credentials and sensitive personal and financial information.

why_concerning.observation: The sender address is security@paypa1-alerts.net — the domain uses the digit '1' where 'paypal' would use the letter 'l'.
why_concerning.why_it_matters: This substitution makes the domain visually resemble the PayPal brand while being an entirely different address. It is a widely recognized technique used to make recipients believe they are hearing from a legitimate sender.

why_concerning.observation: The verification link is http://secure-paypa1-verify.com/restore — the same digit-for-letter substitution appears in the domain, and it uses HTTP rather than HTTPS.
why_concerning.why_it_matters: The domain is not paypal.com. The lookalike spelling, combined with the unencrypted connection, means any information entered there is not being submitted to PayPal and is not protected in transit.

why_concerning.observation: The message demands action within 24 hours and threatens permanent account deletion if you do not comply.
why_concerning.why_it_matters: A hard deadline with a severe consequence is a pressure tactic. It can push recipients to act before they stop to verify whether the message is genuine.

why_concerning.observation: The message asks you to provide your credit card number, CVV, and Social Security Number through the link it supplies.
why_concerning.why_it_matters: This combination of information — card details plus a government identity number — is sufficient for financial fraud and identity theft. Requests for all three in a single form, reached through an unsolicited message, carry serious risk regardless of how the sender presents itself.

what_doesnt_settle_it: The message uses the name 'PayPal Security Team.' That name can be placed in any email by any sender — it does not confirm the message came from PayPal.
The message mentions 'unusual activity' as a reason for suspension. The existence of that explanation does not confirm whether any such activity actually occurred on your real account.

how_to_verify.action: Open a new browser tab and type paypal.com yourself, or open the PayPal app directly from your device.
how_to_verify.reason: This puts you on the real service, not a site the message directed you to. Check whether your account actually shows a suspension or unusual-activity notice there.

how_to_verify.action: Use the contact information found on the real paypal.com site — not any number or address in this message — if you need to speak with someone.
how_to_verify.reason: Any contact channel supplied inside the suspicious message may route back to the same sender.

what_to_do_now: Change your PayPal password immediately using the real paypal.com site or app — not through the link in this message.
If you used the same password on any other account, change it on those accounts as well.
Review your PayPal account for any transactions or changes you did not make, and use the real site's security or dispute options to report anything unfamiliar.
If the form you submitted also included your credit card number, CVV, or Social Security Number, see the guidance below under 'if you already interacted.'

guidance: Because you entered a password into a page reached through this message, treat that password as exposed. Change it on the real PayPal site now, and anywhere else you used the same password.
Check your PayPal account's security settings — look for any sessions, linked devices, or email/phone changes you did not make, and remove or reverse them through the real site.

If the page also asked for your credit card number or CVV and you entered those, contact your card issuer through the number on the back of your card and describe exactly what you shared. Ask what options they have available. Do not promise yourself they will freeze or reimburse — that depends on the institution and circumstances.

If the page asked for your Social Security Number and you entered it, the appropriate protective steps depend on your situation and jurisdiction. A good starting point is to search for the official fraud or identity-theft guidance from your country's consumer protection authority — do not rely on contact information in this message to find that guidance.

avoid: Do not click the link in the message again.
Do not call any phone number or use any contact information supplied in this message.
Do not submit any further information — name, date of birth, card details, or identity numbers — through any link or form this message provided.
important_unknowns: It is not known from the information supplied which fields you actually filled in on that page — whether it was only a password, or also card details and your Social Security Number. The steps you should prioritize depend on that. If you entered financial or identity information beyond the password, treat the card issuer and identity-protection steps as equally urgent.

input.messageText: Sehr geehrter Kunde, Ihr Konto wurde gesperrt. Klicken Sie SOFORT hier: http://paypa1-sicherheit.xyz/login und bestätigen Sie Ihr Passwort und Ihre "Kreditkartendaten", sonst wird Ihr Konto in 24 Stunden dauerhaft gelöscht. Mit freundlichen Grüßen, PayPal Sicherheitsteam.

output.verdict_explanation: Die Nachricht zeigt mehrere Warnsignale: eine gefälschte Domain (paypa1 statt paypal, Endung .xyz, HTTP statt HTTPS), eine 24-Stunden-Drohung, eine Aufforderung zur Passworteingabe und eine Forderung nach Kreditkartendaten über einen externen Link. Die Überprüfung über einen unabhängigen Kanal ist notwendig, bevor Sie einem dieser Anweisungen folgen.

scam_pattern.label: Phishing / Konto-Imitation
scam_pattern.explanation: Die Nachricht imitiert eine offizielle Mitteilung eines bekannten Zahlungsdienstleisters, verbindet eine Sperrungsdrohung mit einer kurzen Frist und fordert die Eingabe sensibler Daten über einen Link.

why_concerning.observation: Die Link-Domain lautet http://paypa1-sicherheit.xyz/login — mit der Ziffer 1 statt des Buchstabens l in 'paypal' und der Endung .xyz statt .com oder .de.
why_concerning.why_it_matters: Diese Schreibweise kann optisch an den echten Markennamen erinnern, ist aber eine andere Domain. Die Endung .xyz und der Zusatz 'sicherheit' sind kein Bestandteil der offiziell bekannten PayPal-Domains. Außerdem wird HTTP statt HTTPS verwendet, was bedeutet, dass eingegebene Daten nicht einmal verschlüsselt übertragen würden.

why_concerning.observation: Die Nachricht setzt eine 24-Stunden-Frist und droht mit dauerhafter Kontolöschung.
why_concerning.why_it_matters: Eine 24-Stunden-Frist soll schnelles Handeln erzwingen, bevor der Empfänger den Link überprüfen kann.

why_concerning.observation: Die Nachricht fordert explizit Passwort und Kreditkartendaten über den bereitgestellten Link.
why_concerning.why_it_matters: Die gleichzeitige Abfrage von Anmeldedaten und Zahlungsinformationen über einen externen Link ist eine besonders risikoreiche Anfrage. Wer diese Daten eingibt, gibt beides in einem einzigen Schritt preis.

why_concerning.observation: Der gesamte Verifizierungsweg — Link, Anweisungen, Kontaktpunkt — stammt ausschließlich aus der Nachricht selbst.
why_concerning.why_it_matters: Der gesamte Verifizierungsweg stammt aus der Nachricht selbst — es gibt keinen unabhängigen Kanal, um die Herkunft zu überprüfen.

what_doesnt_settle_it: Die Nachricht verwendet eine förmliche Anrede und Abschlussfloskel. Das belegt nicht, wer sie tatsächlich gesendet hat.
Die Erwähnung von 'PayPal Sicherheitsteam' ist eine Behauptung in der Nachricht — keine verifizierten Absenderdaten.
Die Nachricht könnte von jedem erstellt worden sein, unabhängig davon, wie sorgfältig sie formuliert ist.

how_to_verify.action: Öffnen Sie die offizielle PayPal-Website, indem Sie die Adresse selbst in die Browserzeile eingeben (z. B. paypal.com), und melden Sie sich dort an.
how_to_verify.reason: Nur so sehen Sie, ob Ihr Konto tatsächlich eingeschränkt ist — ohne den Link aus der Nachricht zu verwenden.

how_to_verify.action: Nutzen Sie alternativ die offizielle PayPal-App, die Sie selbst installiert haben.
how_to_verify.reason: Die App verbindet sich direkt mit PayPal und ist nicht von dieser Nachricht beeinflusst.

how_to_verify.action: Rufen Sie den PayPal-Kundendienst über eine Telefonnummer an, die Sie auf der offiziellen Website oder auf einem früheren Kontoauszug gefunden haben — nicht über eine Nummer, die in dieser Nachricht steht.
how_to_verify.reason: So können Sie direkt bestätigen lassen, ob Ihr Konto gesperrt ist.

what_to_do_now: Klicken Sie nicht auf den Link in der Nachricht.
Geben Sie nirgendwo Ihr Passwort oder Ihre Kreditkartendaten ein, solange Sie nicht über einen unabhängigen Kanal bestätigt haben, dass tatsächlich ein Problem besteht.
Prüfen Sie Ihren Kontostatus direkt über die offizielle PayPal-Website oder App, die Sie selbst aufrufen.

Wenn Sie die Nachricht per E-Mail erhalten haben, können Sie sie als Phishing-Versuch an die zuständige Stelle bei PayPal melden — die entsprechenden Hinweise finden Sie auf der offiziell aufgerufenen PayPal-Website.
avoid: Passwort oder Kreditkartendaten über diesen oder einen anderen in der Nachricht enthaltenen Link eingeben.
Die Nachricht an Dritte weiterzuleiten — falls jemand anderes denselben Link öffnet, ist er denselben Risiken ausgesetzt.
important_unknowns: Über welchen Kanal die Nachricht kam (E-Mail, SMS, Messenger) — das ändert zwar nicht die Warnsignale, kann aber beeinflussen, wo und wie Sie sie melden können.

input.messageText:
Hi David! Sorry for the late reply, this is Wenjing from the tennis club. Is this still your number?

[after reply]

Oh I'm so sorry, wrong number! But you seem nice. I'm new to the area, I moved here from Singapore last year for work. Do you live nearby?

[three days of friendly conversation later]

My uncle works in commodities and he's been helping me with a gold trading account. I made 2,400 last month just following his signals. I'm not trying to sell you anything, I just think you'd be good at it. I can show you the platform if you're curious, no pressure at all.

output.verdict_explanation: The message follows a recognizable sequence: an unsolicited wrong-number opener, several days of relationship-building with no apparent purpose, and then an unsolicited investment opportunity introduced through a personal connection ('my uncle'). Each stage is consistent with a pattern in which rapport is built before a financial platform or opportunity is introduced. No single element confirms fraud, but the combination is strong enough to treat this with serious caution.

input_conflict.note: Your pasted conversation includes '[after reply]' and '[three days of friendly conversation later],' which suggests you replied and continued the exchange over multiple days. You selected 'I haven't interacted,' but the transcript indicates otherwise. The rest of this response is based on what the transcript shows, not the selection, since the transcript is the more specific evidence. If the bracketed labels were added by you to describe a hypothetical scenario rather than something that actually happened, the 'if_you_already_interacted' section may not apply to you.

scam_pattern.label: Romance / Relationship scam leading into investment fraud (sometimes called 'pig butchering')
scam_pattern.explanation: This sequence is consistent with a scam pattern in which an unsolicited contact — often beginning as an apparent wrong number — develops trust over days of friendly conversation, then introduces a profitable-sounding investment opportunity, usually involving a trading platform and a trusted insider (a relative or mentor). The financial opportunity is introduced after the relationship feels natural, which is what makes the ask feel low-pressure and credible. That said, this describes a recognized pattern, not a confirmed fact about this specific sender.

why_concerning.observation: The contact opened with 'Is this still your number?' addressed to a specific name, then immediately pivoted to 'wrong number' after a reply.
why_concerning.why_it_matters: This opener does not require the sender to know anything about the recipient in advance. It can draw a reply from almost anyone who receives it, and the 'wrong number' framing creates a natural reason for the conversation to continue without the recipient feeling targeted.

why_concerning.observation: Three days of personal conversation preceded the investment mention, with no apparent reason other than building familiarity.
why_concerning.why_it_matters: In an ordinary wrong-number exchange, correcting the mistake does not require days of continued personal conversation. The extended rapport-building becomes more significant when it is followed directly by a financial opportunity.

why_concerning.observation: 'My uncle works in commodities and hes been helping me with a gold trading account. I made 2,400 last month just following his signals.'
why_concerning.why_it_matters: A specific, recent profit figure from a trusted insider is a common way to make an investment opportunity feel credible and attainable. It is presented as a personal disclosure, not a sales pitch, which lowers the perceived risk of engaging further.

why_concerning.observation: 'Im not trying to sell you anything' and 'no pressure at all.'
why_concerning.why_it_matters: Explicit reassurances that there is no sales intent can make an approach feel safer than it might otherwise. These phrases do not establish that the offer is legitimate — they address the concern without resolving it.

why_concerning.observation: An offer to 'show you the platform' follows the trust-building stage.
why_concerning.why_it_matters: Introducing a trading platform at this stage fits the pattern in which a fraudulent or manipulated interface is shown only after a relationship has been established. The message does not establish who operates the platform or whether funds placed there can be withdrawn.

what_doesnt_settle_it: The sender's name, location story, and background details are plausible-sounding, but none of that verifies who is actually sending the messages.
The conversation tone is warm and low-pressure. Scam approaches can be low-pressure, especially early on.
A profit figure of 2,400 is specific enough to sound real. Specific numbers do not verify that the account or the returns exist.
The sender has not yet asked for money, credentials, or personal information in the supplied material. That does not mean the contact is safe — in this pattern, those requests typically come later.

how_to_verify.action: Do not attempt to verify through this sender.
how_to_verify.reason: Any information they provide about themselves, the uncle, or the platform comes from the same unverified source.

how_to_verify.action: If the sender claims any connection to a real organization or regulated platform, look up that platform independently and check whether it is registered with the relevant financial regulator in your country.
how_to_verify.reason: Regulated investment platforms are required to be listed with financial authorities. An unregistered platform is a significant warning sign on its own.

how_to_verify.action: Before placing any money on a platform introduced this way, search the platform name alongside terms like 'scam,' 'withdrawal blocked,' or 'fraud' to see what others have reported.
how_to_verify.reason: Platforms used in this pattern often have documented complaints about blocked withdrawals or frozen accounts.

what_to_do_now: Do not send money, transfer cryptocurrency, or deposit funds into any platform this contact introduces.
Do not share financial account details, identity documents, passwords, or one-time codes with this sender.
Do not install any app or software at this sender's suggestion.
If you have already been in conversation: you can disengage at any point. You do not owe an explanation.

guidance: Based on the transcript, you have been in conversation for several days. Conversation by itself does not create financial or account exposure.
The risk rises sharply if the next step involves sending money, depositing into a platform, sharing account credentials, or providing identity documents. Do not take any of those steps.

If you have already deposited money or shared financial information with this sender or a platform they introduced, contact your bank or payment provider promptly through a number on their official website or the back of your card, and describe exactly what happened.

avoid: Sending any money or cryptocurrency to this contact or a platform they introduce.
Sharing bank details, card numbers, identity documents, or login credentials.
Installing apps or clicking links at this sender's direction.
Using any investment platform introduced through this contact without independently verifying it is regulated and has no reported withdrawal problems.
important_unknowns: Whether the bracketed labels in the transcript describe something that actually happened or a hypothetical scenario you constructed — this affects whether the 'if_you_already_interacted' guidance applies to you.
Whether the sender has yet named or linked to a specific platform — the nature of that platform, if introduced, would be relevant to assess further.
